name: policy-guard
aliases: policy decision point / policy enforcement point
intent: Keep every authorisation decision out of the protected resource's code by moving the rules into a separate Policy component and letting a Guard - the enforcement point every access must pass through - obtain a decision from that policy before the operation is performed.
problem: Access rules written inside the resource's own methods (checking roles or ownership inline) entangle business logic with security logic: the same rule is re-implemented at every call site, a forgotten check silently opens a bypass, and the rules cannot be reviewed, tested or changed without touching the resource's code.
context: Components that own protected resources or operations and must decide per access whether the authenticated subject - with its roles, attributes, tenant and request context - may perform the requested action. Typical at object, module or boundary scope: request handlers, domain services, document stores, message consumers and administrative tooling that all reach the same resources and should obey the same rules, especially when the rules change more often than the resource code.
benefits: The security rule changes in one place: a new role, tenant, attribute or resource type is expressed in the Policy and its Rule set instead of being edited into scattered resource methods.
The resource stays free of authorization logic, so resource code can be reviewed for domain correctness and enforcement code for security correctness independently.
Because the Guard sequences the decision before fulfilment and denies by default, a forgotten check becomes structurally visible and auditable rather than silently absent.
One decision component can be unit-tested table-wise over (subject, action, resource, context) cases, which makes rule reasoning, regression testing and review cheap.
Several enforcement points - HTTP API, batch jobs, message consumers, admin tools - share one policy implementation, so all entry points agree on the same rules.
Denial behaviour and audit logging are centralised: the guard can log every denied access uniformly and return consistent errors without leaking resource internals.
tradeoffs: A centralized Policy is a single point of failure and attack: if it is unavailable, stale or subverted, every access decision in the system is wrong, so it must be hardened, made highly available and fail closed.

A time-of-check versus time-of-use gap opens between the decision and the resource access: rights can be revoked in between, so the interval must stay short or be bounded by re-checking long-running operations.

The Rules must speak the same language as the resource's operations and identifiers; new resource types, query paths or bulk operations the policy cannot express remain unprotected (including inference through data it does understand).

Every operation pays the decision cost - context collection, rule evaluation, possibly a remote policy call - and caching decisions trades that cost for an invalidation problem that can keep granting revoked rights.
The guard needs a trustworthy security context threaded to every enforcement point; missing or forged context becomes a new attack surface (confused deputy, anonymous users inheriting rights).

Very extensible policy languages are hard to assure: the more expressiveness the rules gain, the harder it becomes to prove what is actually enforced, so monotonic rules that only grant (with denial by absence) are preferred.

participants.responsibility: Any subject governed by the policy; submits access requests to the Guard and may first authenticate so that its security attributes exist.
Optional component that establishes and verifies the user's identity and makes the subject's attributes available to the security context.

The enforcement point (also known as Policy Enforcement Point): collects the request, target and context attributes, asks the Policy for a decision, rejects requests the policy does not permit, and sequences the check before fulfilment.
The decision component (also known as Policy Decision Point): holds the Rules and decides grant or deny from the subject, request, target and context attributes; it never touches the resource itself.
One entry of the policy expressing which clients may perform which operation on which resource - commonly a (subject, operation, resource) triple, sometimes extended with environmental conditions.
Carries the authenticated subject's credentials and attributes used by the policy decision, from authentication to every guard.
The protected object or operation whose code remains free of authorization logic; it is invoked only after the Guard has obtained a grant.

use_cases: HTTP and API request handling: authentication establishes the security context once, then every endpoint or method invocation is guarded by a policy decision (for example Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind its AuthorizationFilter, or ASP.NET Core authorization middleware over registered policies).

Domain services that expose several operations on one aggregate: the guard checks the (subject, operation, resource) triple before each service method executes, instead of scattering role checks through the methods.
Multi-tenant backends where the decision must consider tenant, ownership and request attributes, not only roles; the guard resolves them from the security context and passes them to the policy.
Document or file stores: every read or write is wrapped by a guard that consults rules keyed by the document identifier and its classification.
Administrative and background code - CLI tools, batch jobs, message consumers - that must obey the same policy as the interactive API so that no side door exists.
Regulated environments where every access decision, including denials, must be logged consistently and the policy itself must be independently testable.

Spring Security request boundaries: AuthorizationFilter passes the current Authentication and HttpServletRequest to an AuthorizationManager and proceeds only after a grant; configure every protected route so an unlisted path cannot become a side door.

ASP.NET Core policy authorization: named policies combine requirements evaluated by IAuthorizationHandler implementations and attach with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization; place UseAuthorization after authentication and before endpoints.

Open Policy Agent (OPA) deployments: AWS Prescriptive Guidance models a centralized or distributed Policy Decision Point with Policy Enforcement Points on APIs, allowing shared policy while using local sidecars when latency or availability requires it.
avoid_when: A platform control already mediates the resource and closes every path to it (API gateway policy enforcement, database row-level security, service-mesh authorization), so an in-process layer would duplicate and could diverge from the effective policy.
The access rule is a constant checked once, or the resource is genuinely public: an inline check - or no check at all - is simpler and more honest than Policy, Guard and Rule components.

You cannot guarantee that every access path crosses a guard (legacy code writes directly to storage, report jobs query the database): establish a single mediation point first (see Reference Monitor) or the guard is decoration.

The operation is a latency-critical inner loop over data that was already authorized at the boundary: authorize once per request and pass the decision along rather than evaluating the policy per element.
anti_patterns: Role or ownership checks sprinkled through the resource's methods: the coupling this pattern removes, with rules invisible to reviewers and impossible to test in isolation.
Enforcement only in the client or UI, or trusting roles, scopes and identifiers supplied in the request body or token without server-side verification.
Fail-open guards: a missing security context, an unavailable policy service or an unrecognised action defaults to allow.
A guard that re-implements the whole rule set as a switch statement while the nominal policy module exists unused - two divergent rule implementations, one of them untested.
Protecting the interactive API while a second code path (reporting job, migration script, message consumer) reaches the same resource directly.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: decision (Policy), enforcement (Guard) and resource behaviour are three distinct responsibilities.
Fail-safe defaults and complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder): deny unless a rule grants access, and check every access through the protected boundary.
Least privilege: rules grant the minimum rights a subject needs for a specific operation and resource.
Open/closed principle: new rules and resource types are added to the policy without editing the resource's code.
Single point of decision and a single enforcement boundary per resource keep the assurance argument small and reviewable.
best_practices: Make the decision function pure and total: for every (subject, action, resource, context) it returns an explicit allow or deny with a reason, and it denies on missing or unknown input.
Keep the guard the only way into the resource - no public back doors - and apply it at the narrowest boundary that every call path must cross.
Express rules as small declarative (subject, action, resource) entries and keep the rule vocabulary aligned with the resource's real operations and identifiers.
Centralise denial handling and audit logging; never let a denied path skip cleanup, mutate state or leak protected data.
Keep the time between decision and use short; re-check authorisation when a request is retried or runs long instead of reusing a stale grant.

Treat the security context as untrusted input to the decision: verify it once at the boundary, make it immutable, and never let the guard use its own server-side privileges on behalf of the user (confused deputy).
Cache decisions only when you can invalidate them precisely, and tie invalidation to the policy change that caused it.
sources: Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering (2005) - the security-pattern catalog the row's provenance is attributed to (Policy and its enforcement point).

The Open Group, Technical Guide: Security Design Patterns (Blakley, Heath et al., 2004), chapter 8.2 Policy (also known as Access Decision Function / Policy Decision Point) and 8.1 Protected System - https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9299969899/toc.pdf
